## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Uttamātherīgāthā* (Thig 3.2) is a short poem in the *Therīgāthā* attributed to the elder nun Uttamā [SuttaCentral]. In these verses, Uttamā describes having repeatedly left her dwelling unable to obtain calm or control over her mind, before approaching a trusted nun for guidance [Shaw 2006]. This preceptor—identified by the commentary as Paṭācārā—instructs her in the Dhamma, detailing the aggregates, sense spheres, and elements [Shaw 2006]. Following these instructions, Uttamā meditates cross-legged for seven days before attaining arahantship, an event captured in the physical image of stretching her legs in liberation [Shaw 2006]. The verses are cited in modern scholarship as an example of a monastic attaining liberation through teaching received from another disciple of the Buddha rather than directly from the Buddha himself [Shaw 2006]. The *Therīgāthā* collection preserves verses attributed to two distinct bhikkhunīs bearing the name Uttamā [Collett 2014].

SuttaCentral records no curated cross-language parallels for this text, though it lists seventeen modern translations across twelve languages, including English versions by Bhikkhu Sujato and Ayya Soma [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus finds no cross-language matches meeting the scoring threshold, but detects extensive Pali-internal text reuse between segments 1.1–4.1 of the poem and its commentary in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* (ThīA 48–49), which details Uttamā's previous lives and spiritual background [Shaw 2006; DharmaNexus].
